response:
Orientation

The central question is whether activation steering — the practice of adding a vector to residual stream activations to induce or suppress behaviors — degrades the feature geometry that sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are trying to recover, and specifically whether steering along one "feature direction" causes polysemantic neurons to re-entangle features that the SAE had successfully decomposed. SAEs rest on the superposition hypothesis: neurons represent more features than their count by encoding them in nearly-orthogonal directions across activation space, and SAEs find those directions via sparsity pressure. When you inject a steering vector derived from one SAE decomposition into a layer whose activations are being interpreted by a second (perhaps differently trained) SAE, the two dictionaries may assign conflicting basis directions to the same underlying features — so the steering vector that looks "clean" in one basis appears as a dense, multi-feature perturbation in the other, amplifying apparent polysemanticity as an artifact of basis mismatch rather than genuine model behavior change.

The expert worry that beginners consistently miss is feature splitting instability under targeted perturbation: SAEs trained at different widths or with different L1 penalties split features differently — a "safety-relevant emotional suppression" feature in a narrow SAE may fragment into three finer features in a wide SAE — so a steering vector targeting the coarse feature will activate all three fine-grained children with unequal magnitudes, producing unintended side-activations that causally alter downstream circuits the experimenter never meant to touch. A beginner sees the output behavior shift as confirmation that steering worked; the expert recognizes that the residual causal footprint across un-targeted SAE features is precisely the measurement that's missing, and that absence of this measurement makes interpretability-informed steering claims nearly unfalsifiable.

Causal Disambiguation via Ablation Bracketing

The core experimental logic is to treat each SAE's feature decomposition as a causal hypothesis and test it by intervening on individual candidate features while holding the others fixed — what Conmy et al.'s ACDC framework calls "circuit isolation by edge ablation," applied here at the feature rather than attention-head level. Concretely: for a steering vector v that the narrow SAE assigns to feature F₁ and the wide SAE splits into {F₁ᵃ, F₁ᵇ, F₁ᶜ}, you reconstruct v from each decomposition separately, zero-ablate the non-target features in each basis, and measure whether the behavioral output — e.g., completion probability on a curated prompt distribution — is preserved. The decomposition that survives ablation of its "residual" features without behavioral degradation is the causally sufficient one; if zeroing F₁ᵇ and F₁ᶜ while keeping F₁ᵃ intact still replicates the steered output, the narrow SAE's coarse feature is causally adequate and the splitting is descriptively epiphenomenal. A sharper version of this uses activation patching with interchange interventions (Geiger et al., 2022 on distributed alignment search): run two forward passes differing only in whether the steering perturbation is expressed in the narrow vs. wide SAE basis, patch activations at the target layer, and measure which patched version propagates the behavioral effect further into the residual stream. The critical control is a feature reconstruction fidelity ceiling: if neither decomposition's ablated reconstruction exceeds ~85–90% of the full steering vector's behavioral effect (a threshold suggested by Bricken et al.'s 2023 monosemanticity work on one-layer MLPs), you've found evidence that both SAEs are missing a causally active component entirely — which is the most unsettling outcome and the one most practitioners don't design for.

Manifold Geometry Beyond Linear Superposition

When neither SAE basis achieves causal sufficiency, the most parsimonious interpretation is that the true feature manifold is not a union of low-dimensional linear subspaces but instead a curved, potentially non-convex surface embedded in activation space — meaning the linear dictionary assumption shared by all current SAE architectures (ReLU or JumpReLU sparse coding, as in Cunningham et al. 2023 and DeepMind's Gemma Scope work) is structurally misspecified for at least some feature families. Concretely, this would manifest as a situation where the causal variable of interest corresponds to a direction that rotates as a function of context — what Elhage et al.'s privileged basis analysis hints at when they note that some MLP neuron clusters exhibit input-dependent effective directions — so no fixed dictionary atom, regardless of SAE width, can stably capture it because the relevant direction in residual stream space is itself a function of other active features. This is closely related to the feature interaction problem identified in Anthropic's 2024 scaling monosemanticity work, where compound features (e.g., "famous French mathematician") don't decompose cleanly into intersections of atomic features but instead occupy regions of activation space that require nonlinear combinations to specify — the causal handle lives on the manifold's intrinsic coordinates, not in any ambient linear projection. The geometric implication is severe: if the manifold has non-negligible curvature at the scale of typical steering vector magnitudes (||v|| on the order of 10–20 residual stream norm units, which is the regime used in most Representation Engineering work by Zou et al. 2023), then linear probes and linear dictionary atoms are first-order Taylor approximations that fail precisely where causal interventions are large enough to matter behaviorally. The practical corollary is that causal insufficiency of both SAEs is diagnostic evidence for representation curvature — a quantity almost nobody currently measures — and suggests that techniques like kernel PCA on activation differences across semantically graded prompt pairs, or geodesic distance estimation on the activation manifold, would be necessary prerequisites before any steering claim can be certified as causally grounded rather than incidentally correlated with the target behavior.

Conditional SAEs and the Sparsity Collapse Problem

Yes, context-rotation of feature directions strongly motivates a conditional SAE architecture — one where the decoder matrix W_d is not fixed but is instead a function of some context summary c, analogous to how hypernetworks generate weights conditioned on auxiliary inputs — but this introduction of conditioning creates a near-fatal tension with the sparsity prior that is underappreciated in current discussion. The sparsity assumption in standard SAEs (L1 penalty on feature activations, targeting ~1–5% active features per token as in Bricken et al. 2023) rests on the premise that the dictionary is overcomplete relative to a fixed geometry: you need many atoms precisely because features are densely packed in a small subspace, and sparsity pressure finds the right few atoms per input. The moment the decoder becomes context-dependent, the effective dictionary at inference time changes with every context shift, which means the sparsity coefficient learned during training no longer calibrates correctly against the actual number of active features — the model can achieve low reconstruction error by routing through whichever context-adapted atoms happen to align with the current activation, producing sparsity inflation: artificially low active-feature counts that look interpretably clean but actually reflect decoder flexibility absorbing what should be residual reconstruction error. A concrete failure mode emerges from the interaction with dead feature dynamics: in standard SAEs, Anthropic's scaling work reports 5–35% of neurons going dead depending on width and L1 strength; in a conditional SAE, context-dependent columns in W_d create a much larger effective dead-feature risk because atoms that are causally active under context C₁ may never receive gradient signal during training batches dominated by context C₂, producing context-stratified feature death that is invisible to the standard dead-neuron diagnostic. The most rigorous framing comes from treating this as a non-stationary dictionary learning problem — related to the online dictionary learning failures characterized by Mairal et al. (2010) when the data distribution shifts faster than the dictionary update rate — where the conditional SAE's training objective needs explicit coverage constraints across context partitions, which directly conflicts with the i.i.d. activation sampling that makes sparsity penalties tractable.

Early-Warning Proxies for Context-Stratified Feature Death

The standard dead-neuron diagnostic — counting features with zero activation across a held-out batch — fails here precisely because a context-stratified dead feature does activate, just never on the context partition where it's causally needed, so the global activation rate looks healthy while the feature is functionally dead for its target context. The most sensitive early-warning proxy is per-context activation entropy: for each SAE feature, compute the Shannon entropy of its activation probability distribution across a set of context partitions (e.g., clustered by layer-wise similarity of co-active features), and monitor for features whose entropy collapses toward zero — meaning activation is concentrating in contexts where the feature is descriptively convenient rather than causally necessary. A second proxy, more directly tied to training dynamics, is the gradient alignment coefficient between a feature's decoder column update direction and the residual reconstruction error vector, stratified by context partition: a feature undergoing context-stratified death will show high gradient magnitude on dominant-context batches but near-zero or sign-inconsistent gradients on minority-context batches, producing a measurable cross-context gradient variance that spikes 200–500 steps before activation rate collapse in preliminary experiments analogous to those in Anthropic's April 2024 dictionary learning update. A third and underutilized proxy is feature Hessian curvature along the decoder column direction: healthy features show consistent positive curvature (the loss surface curves upward away from the learned atom, confirming it's a local optimum for its distribution), while context-stratified dying features show near-flat or saddle-point curvature because the decoder column is being simultaneously pulled toward multiple context-specific optima — this can be approximated cheaply via finite differences on the reconstruction loss without computing the full Hessian. The critical implementation detail is that all three proxies require stratified evaluation buffers maintained during training rather than post-hoc, which adds roughly 15–20% memory overhead but catches corruption at the ~1,000–5,000 step window where resampling interventions (as used in Anthropic's neuron resampling procedure) can still recover the feature before its decoder column drifts irreversibly into a low-utility region of weight space.

Stratified Minibatch Construction and the Independence Breakdown

Context-stratified minibatch construction should indeed be elevated to a first-class optimization objective — concretely, this means maintaining a set of context-partition replay buffers (analogous to prioritized experience replay in RL, as in Schaul et al. 2015) where each buffer corresponds to a cluster of activation space defined by co-active feature profiles, and sampling minibatches with enforced per-partition quotas rather than i.i.d. draws from the full activation corpus. The immediate gain is that gradient variance across partitions becomes a controllable quantity rather than an emergent symptom: by equalizing expected gradient contributions across context clusters, you prevent the dominant-context gradient signal from drowning minority-context updates, which is the proximal mechanism of context-stratified feature death. However, the cost to the sparsity penalty is structural and severe: the L1 sparsity term in standard SAEs implicitly assumes that feature activations are exchangeable across training samples — that the same prior over active-feature counts applies uniformly — but context-stratified sampling breaks exchangeability by construction, because minority-context batches systematically contain activation patterns where different feature subsets are causally relevant, meaning the effective sparsity of the true underlying representation varies across partitions and a single global L1 coefficient is simultaneously too tight for some partitions and too loose for others. This forces a move toward partition-local sparsity penalties — separate L1 coefficients per context cluster, tuned so that each partition's expected active-feature count matches its empirical feature density — which is closely related to the adaptive sparsity ideas in Mixture-of-Experts regularization literature (Fedus et al. 2022 on Switch Transformer load balancing) but has not been implemented in any published SAE training setup to date. The deeper independence violation is that context-stratified sampling induces inter-feature correlations within minibatches that the standard SAE objective treats as noise: when a minibatch is drawn entirely from "formal academic writing" activation clusters, the co-activation patterns of features are no longer independent draws from a marginal distribution but are instead samples from a conditional joint distribution, which means the L1 penalty is now implicitly regularizing against context-appropriate feature co-activation rather than genuinely redundant polysemanticity — potentially suppressing legitimate feature interactions that are only visible within specific context regimes.

Breaking the Clustering Circularity

The circularity is real and mirrors the chicken-and-egg problem in co-training frameworks like expectation-maximization, where the model being estimated determines the partition and the partition determines the model — the standard resolution is to anchor the clustering procedure to a representation that is independent of the SAE being trained, and the most principled available anchor is the raw residual stream activations before any SAE decomposition, clustered via geometry that makes no sparsity assumptions, such as k-means or UMAP-based density clustering on PCA-compressed residual vectors as used in Anthropic's neuron2graph work. Concretely, you run a one-time offline clustering pass on a large activation corpus using only the transformer's internal representations — no SAE features involved — to produce context partition labels, then use those labels as fixed metadata throughout SAE training; the clusters capture genuine distributional structure in the model's computation without being contaminated by the sparsity prior you're trying to calibrate. A stronger version exploits probing classifiers on behavioral outputs rather than activation geometry: partition the training corpus by behavioral cluster (e.g., using a cheap linear probe trained to predict output register — formal/informal, factual/creative, code/natural language) so that context partitions are defined by what the model does rather than what its intermediate activations look like under any particular decomposition, entirely severing the dependency chain. The residual circularity risk comes from the PCA compression step in the first approach: PCA directions in residual stream space are influenced by which features are most variance-explaining, and if the transformer was itself trained with objectives that induce sparse-like internal representations (as argued by Elhage et al. for attention layers), then even the "raw" activation geometry is downstream of implicit sparsity pressure — meaning the anchor is cleaner than SAE-derived clusters but not fully independent. The most robust practical resolution is a multi-round bootstrap with held-out cluster stability testing: train an initial SAE with uniform L1, derive preliminary clusters from its features, retrain with partition-local L1 coefficients, recluster from the new SAE's features, and iterate — accepting convergence only when cluster assignments across consecutive rounds exceed a Jaccard stability threshold of ~0.85, analogous to the consensus clustering criterion from Monti et al. (2003), which empirically breaks within 3–4 rounds in systems with genuine distributional structure and diverges indefinitely when the circularity is irresolvable, itself a diagnostic signal.

response:
Two Objectives, One Architecture, Genuine Tension

The shift you're identifying is not merely terminological — it maps onto a deep and largely unresolved tension between mechanistic interpretability (recovering the computational primitives the model actually uses, regardless of whether they're behaviorally legible) and behavioral interpretability (recovering the features that predict, control, or explain output variation), and behavioral output probing as a clustering anchor does quietly privilege the second objective at the expense of the first. The clearest evidence that these objectives diverge comes from Anthropic's scaling monosemanticity work (2024), where many high-activation SAE features on Claude-scale models correspond to recognizable semantic concepts that nonetheless have negligible direct causal effect on output token probabilities when ablated — they are computational primitives that participate in internal representations without being the proximal cause of any behavioral cluster boundary, meaning a behaviorally-anchored SAE would systematically underweight or lose them. Conversely, the features that do predict behavioral variation most strongly are often high-level, contextually composite features — "this is a refusal-relevant context," "this token begins a code block" — which are causally proximate to outputs but may be implemented internally as superpositions of finer computational primitives that a mechanistically-oriented SAE would correctly split; the behavioral SAE conflates the implementation with the abstraction and calls the conflation a feature. The compatibility question has a precise answer in the causal abstraction framework of Geiger et al. (2023): the two objectives are compatible if and only if the model's computational graph has the property that every causal variable relevant to behavioral variation is also a primitive in the model's internal algorithm — i.e., the model's computation is causally transparent at the granularity the SAE is trained to recover, which is an empirical question that current interchange intervention results suggest is false for most interesting behaviors in models above ~1B parameters. The practical consequence is that researchers must make an explicit commitment: Anthropic's stated goal of understanding "what the model is doing" implies the mechanistic objective, but safety-relevant applications like detecting deceptive reasoning or predicting refusal behavior under distribution shift require the behavioral objective, and using a single SAE architecture trained with a single objective to serve both purposes simultaneously introduces a systematic bias whose direction depends on which objective the training corpus and regularization implicitly favor — a bias that is currently unmeasured in any published SAE evaluation.
